PAGE 1: Overview

OVERVIEW
========

Family celebrations use words such as birthday, party, gift and joy. In this sub-strand you will hear and say the sounds /ɜː/, /ɑː/, /ɔɪ/, /aɪ/, /l/ and /r/, build celebration words, and use them in clear sentences.

## Strand 2.0: Family Celebrations
Sub-strand 2.1.1: Listening and Speaking: Pronunciation and Vocabulary
Suggested lessons: 3

## What this sub-strand covers
• Target sounds

## Source
• KICD Grade 4 English Language Curriculum Design (Revised 2024) — Theme 2.0 Family Celebrations, Sub-strand 2.1.1 Pronunciation and Vocabulary

## Learning outcomes
By the end of the sub-strand, the learner should be able to:
a) discriminate sounds and words for listening, comprehension
b) pronounce words containing target sounds accurately for effective communication
c) appreciate the importance of accurate pronunciation for effective communication

## Key inquiry questions
1. Why should you pronounce sounds and words correctly?
2. Which words are used as subjects in a sentence?

PAGE 2: How we will learn

## Learning experiences
• listen to a variety of audio materials and identify sounds (/ɜː/ /ɑː/ /ɔɪ/ /aɪ/ / l/ /r/), words and expressions related to the theme
• listen to a passage or dialogue read by the teacher and identify the sounds /ɜː/ /ɑː/ /ɔɪ/ /aɪ/ / l/ /r/
• use vocabulary related to the theme to construct a variety of sentences
• team up to use word wheels with sounds /ɜː/ /ɑː/ /ɔɪ/ /aɪ/ / l/ /r/ to form new words such as load, road, boy, toy
• watch a video together from the web offline or online and identify target sounds and words
• role play and create a video collaboratively using the learnt sounds and words

## Core competencies
• Communication and Collaboration: This is enhanced as the learner role-plays and creates a video collaboratively using learnt sounds and words.
• Digital Literacy: The skills are developed as the learner watches a video and identifies words with target sounds.

## Values
• Unity: This is enhanced as the learner cooperates with peers to use word wheels to form new words with target sounds.
• Love: It is developed as the learner displays an attitude of care for others as they work together.

## Pertinent and contemporary issues
• Social cohesion: This is developed as the learner works together with peers harmoniously to complete tasks.

## Links to other learning areas
• The learner is able to relate the concept of pronunciation to their learning in Kiswahili.

PAGE 3: Lesson 1: Hearing the sounds /ɜː/, /ɑː/, /ɔɪ/ and /aɪ/

LESSON 1: HEARING THE SOUNDS /Ɜː/, /Ɑː/, /ƆꞮ/ AND /AꞮ/
======================================================

## What you will learn
• Hear the difference between /ɜː/, /ɑː/, /ɔɪ/ and /aɪ/.
• Say words that contain each target sound.
• Match celebration words to the sound they contain.

Curriculum outcomes: a) discriminate sounds and words for listening, comprehension; b) pronounce words containing target sounds accurately for effective communication

## Introduction
The words boy and buy are easy to mix up if you hurry. Boy names a male child. Buy means to pay for something. The vowel sound in the middle is what keeps the two words apart.

PAGE 4: Lesson 1: Hearing the sounds /ɜː/, /ɑː/, /ɔɪ/ and /aɪ/ — /ɜː/ as in birthday

## Notes

### Sounds, not just letters
In this lesson a sound is written between slanting lines, like /ɔɪ/. The lines mean we are talking about what we hear, not about one spelling. The same sound can be spelled in more than one way.

### /ɜː/ as in birthday
/ɜː/ is the long vowel in bird, girl, birthday, turn, word and her. Your mouth is relaxed and the sound is held. You often see it spelled ir (birthday, girl), ur (turn, church), or (word) or er (her).

Say: birthday, girl, turn, her, church.

### /ɑː/ as in father
/ɑː/ is the long "ah" in father, party, card and start. Open your mouth and keep the sound long. You often see it spelled ar (card, start, arm) or a (father, party).

Say: father, party, card, start.

Do not swap /ɜː/ and /ɑː/. Birthday has /ɜː/. Party has /ɑː/. They are different vowels even though both can be long.

PAGE 5: Lesson 1: Hearing the sounds /ɜː/, /ɑː/, /ɔɪ/ and /aɪ/ — /aɪ/ as in prize

### /ɔɪ/ as in boy
/ɔɪ/ glides. Start with the vowel in "or" and move toward the vowel in "see". You hear it in boy, toy, joy, coin and voice. The usual spellings are oy (boy, toy, joy) and oi (coin, voice).

### /aɪ/ as in prize
/aɪ/ also glides. Start with "ah" and move toward "ee". You hear it in my, prize, invite, time and night. Spellings include i (prize, invite, time), y (my) and igh (night).

### Hear the difference
- boy /ɔɪ/ and buy /aɪ/
- toy /ɔɪ/ and tie /aɪ/
- birthday /ɜː/ and party /ɑː/

PAGE 6: Lesson 1: Hearing the sounds /ɜː/, /ɑː/, /ɔɪ/ and /aɪ/ — Celebration words with these vowels

### Celebration words with these vowels
- birthday, church (/ɜː/)
- party, father, card (/ɑː/)
- boy, toy, joy (/ɔɪ/)
- invite, prize, night (/aɪ/)

When you listen to a story about a party, tap once for /ɔɪ/ and twice for /aɪ/. Training your ear is the first step to saying the words clearly.

## Key words
• /ɜː/ — the long vowel sound in birthday, bird and turn
• /ɑː/ — the long ah sound in father, party and card
• /ɔɪ/ — the vowel sound in boy, toy and joy
• /aɪ/ — the vowel sound in my, prize and invite

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Which word has /ɔɪ/: boy, buy or card?

Working:
1. Boy has the oy spelling and the /ɔɪ/ sound.
2. Buy has /aɪ/. Card has /ɑː/.

Answer: boy

## Worked examples

### Example 2
Sort these words by vowel sound: birthday, party, joy, prize.

Working:
1. Birthday has /ɜː/.
2. Party has /ɑː/.
3. Joy has /ɔɪ/.
4. Prize has /aɪ/.

Answer: /ɜː/ birthday; /ɑː/ party; /ɔɪ/ joy; /aɪ/ prize

PAGE 7: Lesson 1: Hearing the sounds /ɜː/, /ɑː/, /ɔɪ/ and /aɪ/ — Listen and sort the vowels

## Activity: Listen and sort the vowels
You will need: Four cards labelled /ɜː/, /ɑː/, /ɔɪ/ and /aɪ/, A list of words read aloud by the teacher or played from an audio recording

1. Listen to each word once: birthday, girl, party, father, card, boy, toy, joy, invite, prize, night, turn.

2. Point to the card for the vowel sound you hear. Do not look at a spelling until you have chosen.

3. Say the word after the teacher, matching the length of the vowel.

4. With a partner, say boy and buy, then toy and tie, and explain the meaning of each word.

PAGE 8: Lesson 1: Hearing the sounds /ɜː/, /ɑː/, /ɔɪ/ and /aɪ/ — Summary

## Practice

1. Write the sound symbol for the vowel in joy.

2. Which word does not have /aɪ/: invite, prize, night, coin?

3. Say whether birthday and party have the same vowel sound. Name both sounds.

4. What is the difference in meaning between boy and buy?

## Answers to practice

1. /ɔɪ/

2. coin (coin has /ɔɪ/)

3. No. Birthday has /ɜː/ and party has /ɑː/.

4. A boy is a male child. To buy is to pay for something.

## Summary
• /ɜː/ is the vowel in birthday. /ɑː/ is the vowel in father and party.
• /ɔɪ/ is the vowel in boy and joy. /aɪ/ is the vowel in prize and invite.
• Hear the sound before you worry about the spelling.

PAGE 9: Lesson 2: The sounds /l/ and /r/ and celebration words

LESSON 2: THE SOUNDS /L/ AND /R/ AND CELEBRATION WORDS
======================================================

## What you will learn
• Hear and say /l/ and /r/ at the beginning of words.
• Use word wheels to build words such as load and road.
• Explain celebration words and use four of them in sentences.

Curriculum outcomes: a) discriminate sounds and words for listening, comprehension; b) pronounce words containing target sounds accurately for effective communication

## Introduction
If someone says "Turn light at the gate" when they mean "Turn right", the visitor walks the wrong way. The sounds /l/ and /r/ are different, and a celebration direction can depend on them.

## Notes

### How to make /l/
Put the tip of your tongue on the ridge behind your top teeth and let the air pass along the sides. Your voice is on. You hear /l/ at the start of load, light, play, balloon, colourful and celebrate.

### How to make /r/
Keep the tongue tip from touching that ridge. The tongue pulls back a little and the voice stays on. You hear /r/ at the start of road, right, pray, ribbon, present and prize.

Do not press your lips together for either sound. If /r/ starts to sound like /w/, smile slightly and keep the tongue busy.

PAGE 10: Lesson 2: The sounds /l/ and /r/ and celebration words — Word wheels

### Pairs that change meaning
- load and road
- light and right
- play and pray
- glass and grass
- lock and rock

Load means to put things onto a vehicle or a table. Road means the way vehicles travel. A wedding party can load gifts into a car and then travel on the road. Both words matter.

### Word wheels
A word wheel has a sound in the centre and letters around the edge. Join the centre to different letters to make words.

- Centre /l/: load, light, lock
- Centre /r/: road, right, rock
- Centre /ɔɪ/: boy, toy, joy
- Centre /aɪ/: my can be built by adding letters around the sound in prize, invite and night

PAGE 11: Lesson 2: The sounds /l/ and /r/ and celebration words — Words for family celebrations

### Words for family celebrations
- celebrate: to mark a special day with happy activities
- ceremony: a set of formal actions for an important event
- invitation: a request, spoken or written, asking someone to come
- wedding: the ceremony when two people marry
- birthday: the day each year that marks when a person was born
- burial: the ceremony of laying to rest a person who has died. Families gather, sing and comfort one another.
- feast: a large special meal
- graduation: a ceremony at the end of a level of school
- baptise: in many Christian families, a ceremony that welcomes a person, often a baby, with water
- decorate: to make a place look special
- Other useful words: ribbon, balloon, gift, present, card, cake, prize, song, joy

PAGE 12: Lesson 2: The sounds /l/ and /r/ and celebration words — Key words

A present and a gift can mean the same thing: something you give. A prize is something you win.

Use a word in a full sentence so its meaning shows: We will decorate the room with balloons and ribbons for the birthday party.

## Key words
• ceremony — a set of formal actions for an important event such as a wedding
• invitation — a request asking someone to come to an event
• feast — a large special meal for a celebration
• decorate — to add colours and objects that make a place look special

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Which word begins with /r/: balloon, ribbon, colourful, celebrate?

Working:
1. Balloon, colourful and celebrate begin with other sounds or have /l/.
2. Ribbon begins with /r/.

Answer: ribbon

## Worked examples

### Example 2
Use invitation and feast in one sentence about a wedding.

Working:
1. An invitation asks people to come.
2. A feast is the special meal.
3. Join them with a wedding.

Answer: Our invitation to the wedding said there would be a feast after the ceremony.

PAGE 13: Lesson 2: The sounds /l/ and /r/ and celebration words — Word wheels for /l/ and /r/

## Activity: Word wheels for /l/ and /r/
You will need: Paper circles divided into wedges, Pencils, A list of celebration words

1. In a group, draw two wheels. Write /l/ in the centre of one and /r/ in the centre of the other.

2. Around /l/ write load, light, lock, balloon and play. Around /r/ write road, right, rock, ribbon and prize.

3. Say each pair, load/road and light/right, and point to the wheel you hear when a partner says one word.

4. Choose four celebration words and each say a sentence that uses one of them.

PAGE 14: Lesson 2: The sounds /l/ and /r/ and celebration words — Answers to practice

## Practice

1. Write the /r/ partner of load, light and lock.

2. What is the difference between a gift and a prize?

3. Use the word decorate in a sentence about a birthday.

4. Which sound starts ribbon: /l/ or /r/?

## Answers to practice

1. road, right, rock

2. A gift is something you give to someone. A prize is something a person wins.

3. Any correct sentence, for example: We will decorate the room with balloons for the birthday party.

4. /r/

## Summary
• /l/ touches the tooth ridge. /r/ does not.
• Pairs such as load and road change meaning when the first sound changes.
• Celebration words include ceremony, invitation, feast, decorate, gift and prize.

PAGE 15: Lesson 3: Clear words in a celebration dialogue — A dialogue to listen to

LESSON 3: CLEAR WORDS IN A CELEBRATION DIALOGUE
===============================================

## What you will learn
• Pronounce target sounds in a short dialogue.
• Say why a wrong sound can confuse a listener.
• Role-play a celebration using the new words.

Curriculum outcomes: b) pronounce words containing target sounds accurately for effective communication; c) appreciate the importance of accurate pronunciation for effective communication

## Introduction
A family is planning a birthday. Every person in the plan must be heard correctly: who to invite, what to buy, and where to put the ribbons. Clear sounds keep the plan from falling apart.

## Notes

### A dialogue to listen to
Ask your teacher or a partner to read this aloud. Listen for /ɜː/, /ɑː/, /ɔɪ/, /aɪ/, /l/ and /r/.

Mother: We will have a party for your birthday.
Amina: May I invite my friends?
Mother: Yes. We can decorate the room with balloons and ribbons.
Father: I will buy a card and a gift. I will not forget the prize for the game.
Amina: Will there be a cake?
Mother: Yes, and we will sing a song. It will be a day of joy.
Father: Load the chairs onto the path, then carry them to the right side of the yard.

PAGE 16: Lesson 3: Clear words in a celebration dialogue — Why clear pronunciation matters

### Sounds in the dialogue
- party /ɑː/, birthday /ɜː/
- invite /aɪ/, buy /aɪ/, prize /aɪ/, right /aɪ/ and /r/
- joy /ɔɪ/
- balloons /l/, load /l/
- ribbons /r/, prize /r/, right /r/

Say the dialogue slowly, then at a natural speed. If you add the line "The boy will buy the balloons", keep boy and buy distinct.

### Why clear pronunciation matters
A listener cannot see your spelling. They only hear sounds. Load and road, light and right, boy and buy are different messages. At a celebration, the wrong word can send people, gifts or chairs to the wrong place.

Clear speech also shows respect. Guests who are older, younger, or visiting from another place should not have to struggle to understand you. Everyone's voice is a little different, and that is welcome. What we aim for is that the important sounds stay distinct.

PAGE 17: Lesson 3: Clear words in a celebration dialogue — Key words

### Subjects in these sentences
The key question for this theme also asks which words are used as subjects. In "Amina will invite her friends", Amina is the subject: she does the action. In "Father will buy a card", Father is the subject. The subject is usually the person or thing the sentence is about, and it often comes before the verb. Naming the subject clearly is part of speaking so that others understand.

### After you speak
When you role-play, face your partners, speak loudly enough for the group, and leave a pause at the full stop. If someone mishears right as light, repeat the word once, kindly, and show the direction with your hand.

## Key words
• dialogue — a conversation written so that each speaker has a turn
• subject — the person or thing that does the action in a sentence
• pronounce — to say a sound or word in a particular way

PAGE 18: Lesson 3: Clear words in a celebration dialogue — Example 2

## Worked examples

### Example 1
In the dialogue, who is the subject of "I will buy a card and a gift"?

Working:
1. The speaker of that line is Father.
2. I stands for Father.
3. Father is the person who will buy.

Answer: Father (the word I)

## Worked examples

### Example 2
A learner says "Turn light" but means the opposite of left. Which word should be used, and which sound starts it?

Working:
1. The opposite of left in a direction is right.
2. Right begins with /r/ and has the vowel /aɪ/.

Answer: right, beginning with /r/

PAGE 19: Lesson 3: Clear words in a celebration dialogue — Role-play the birthday plan

## Activity: Role-play the birthday plan
You will need: Copies of the dialogue, Simple props such as a card, a ribbon or a paper balloon, A phone or tablet only if the teacher is recording

1. Listen to the dialogue read aloud or played from an audio recording. List five words with the target sounds.

2. In groups of three, take the parts of Mother, Amina and Father and read the dialogue.

3. Add two new sentences that use celebration words, with a clear subject in each.

4. Role-play the scene. If the teacher agrees, record a short video and watch it to check the sounds /l/ and /r/ and the vowels /ɔɪ/ and /aɪ/.

5. Tell the class why saying load and road differently matters.

PAGE 20: Lesson 3: Clear words in a celebration dialogue — Answers to practice

## Practice

1. Name the target vowel in party and the target vowel in birthday.

2. From the dialogue, write one word with /l/ and one word with /r/.

3. Why should we pronounce sounds and words correctly at a celebration?

4. Who is the subject in "Amina will invite her friends"?

## Answers to practice

1. Party has /ɑː/. Birthday has /ɜː/.

2. Any correct pair, for example balloons (/l/) and ribbons (/r/).

3. So that listeners understand the right message. One wrong sound can change the word, as in light and right.

4. Amina

## Summary
• The dialogue practises /ɜː/, /ɑː/, /ɔɪ/, /aɪ/, /l/ and /r/ in real celebration words.
• A changed sound can change the meaning, so listeners need clear speech.
• The subject is the person or thing that the sentence is about.

PAGE 21: Revision quiz

REVISION QUIZ
=============

Answer all the questions, then mark yourself on the Answers tab.

1. Which word has the vowel /ɔɪ/?
   A. prize
   B. boy
   C. card
   D. birthday

2. Which pair contrasts /l/ and /r/?
   A. boy and toy
   B. load and road
   C. party and father
   D. night and prize

3. Which word begins with /r/?
   A. balloon
   B. celebrate
   C. ribbon
   D. colourful

4. The vowel in invite is ____.
   A. /ɜː/
   B. /ɑː/
   C. /ɔɪ/
   D. /aɪ/

5. What does feast mean?
   A. A written invitation
   B. A large special meal
   C. A prize won in a game
   D. A song sung at night

6. Choose the sentence that uses invitation correctly.
   A. We ate the invitation with a spoon.
   B. The invitation asked us to come to the wedding.
   C. He kicked the invitation into the goal.
   D. The invitation was a tall tree.

7. Why does saying light instead of right cause a problem?

8. Who is the subject in "Father will buy a card"?
   A. card
   B. buy
   C. Father
   D. a

9. Which word has /ɜː/?
   A. party
   B. start
   C. girl
   D. joy

10. Why is clear pronunciation a sign of respect at a family celebration?

PAGE 22: Quiz answers

ANSWERS
=======

1. B. boy
   Boy has /ɔɪ/. Prize has /aɪ/, card has /ɑː/, and birthday has /ɜː/.

2. B. load and road
   Load begins with /l/ and road begins with /r/.

3. C. ribbon
   Ribbon begins with /r/. The other words contain /l/.

4. D. /aɪ/
   Invite has the glide /aɪ/, the same vowel as prize and night.

5. B. A large special meal
   A feast is a large special meal, often part of a celebration.

6. B. The invitation asked us to come to the wedding.
   An invitation asks someone to attend an event.

7. The listener hears a different word and may go the wrong way or misunderstand the message.
   Light and right are different words because /l/ and /r/ are different sounds.

8. C. Father
   Father is the person who does the action.

9. C. girl
   Girl has /ɜː/, like birthday and turn.

10. Guests can understand you without struggling, including people who are younger, older or visiting.
   The aim is distinct sounds so the message is easy to follow.

studyPages.body:
## Notes

### /ɜː/ as in birthday

Say: birthday, girl, turn, her, church.

/ɑː/ is the long "ah" in father, party, card and start. Open your mouth and keep the sound long. You often see it spelled ar (card, start, arm) or a (father, party).

Say: father, party, card, start.

Do not swap /ɜː/ and /ɑː/. Birthday has /ɜː/. Party has /ɑː/. They are different vowels even though both can be long.

studyPages.title: Lesson 1: Hearing the sounds /ɜː/, /ɑː/, /ɔɪ/ and /aɪ/ — /aɪ/ as in prize
studyPages.body:
### /ɔɪ/ as in boy
/ɔɪ/ glides. Start with the vowel in "or" and move toward the vowel in "see". You hear it in boy, toy, joy, coin and voice. The usual spellings are oy (boy, toy, joy) and oi (coin, voice).

### /aɪ/ as in prize
/aɪ/ also glides. Start with "ah" and move toward "ee". You hear it in my, prize, invite, time and night. Spellings include i (prize, invite, time), y (my) and igh (night).

### Hear the difference
- boy /ɔɪ/ and buy /aɪ/
- toy /ɔɪ/ and tie /aɪ/
- birthday /ɜː/ and party /ɑː/

studyPages.title: Lesson 1: Hearing the sounds /ɜː/, /ɑː/, /ɔɪ/ and /aɪ/ — Celebration words with these vowels
studyPages.body:
### Celebration words with these vowels
- birthday, church (/ɜː/)
- party, father, card (/ɑː/)
- boy, toy, joy (/ɔɪ/)
- invite, prize, night (/aɪ/)

When you listen to a story about a party, tap once for /ɔɪ/ and twice for /aɪ/. Training your ear is the first step to saying the words clearly.

## Key words
• /ɜː/ — the long vowel sound in birthday, bird and turn
• /ɑː/ — the long ah sound in father, party and card
• /ɔɪ/ — the vowel sound in boy, toy and joy
• /aɪ/ — the vowel sound in my, prize and invite

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Which word has /ɔɪ/: boy, buy or card?

Working:
1. Boy has the oy spelling and the /ɔɪ/ sound.
2. Buy has /aɪ/. Card has /ɑː/.

Answer: boy

## Worked examples

### Example 2
Sort these words by vowel sound: birthday, party, joy, prize.

Working:
1. Birthday has /ɜː/.
2. Party has /ɑː/.
3. Joy has /ɔɪ/.
4. Prize has /aɪ/.

Answer: /ɜː/ birthday; /ɑː/ party; /ɔɪ/ joy; /aɪ/ prize

studyPages.title: Lesson 1: Hearing the sounds /ɜː/, /ɑː/, /ɔɪ/ and /aɪ/ — Listen and sort the vowels
studyPages.body:
## Activity: Listen and sort the vowels
You will need: Four cards labelled /ɜː/, /ɑː/, /ɔɪ/ and /aɪ/, A list of words read aloud by the teacher or played from an audio recording

1. Listen to each word once: birthday, girl, party, father, card, boy, toy, joy, invite, prize, night, turn.

2. Point to the card for the vowel sound you hear. Do not look at a spelling until you have chosen.

3. Say the word after the teacher, matching the length of the vowel.

4. With a partner, say boy and buy, then toy and tie, and explain the meaning of each word.

studyPages.title: Lesson 1: Hearing the sounds /ɜː/, /ɑː/, /ɔɪ/ and /aɪ/ — Summary
studyPages.body:
## Practice

1. Write the sound symbol for the vowel in joy.

2. Which word does not have /aɪ/: invite, prize, night, coin?

3. Say whether birthday and party have the same vowel sound. Name both sounds.

4. What is the difference in meaning between boy and buy?

## Answers to practice

1. /ɔɪ/

2. coin (coin has /ɔɪ/)

3. No. Birthday has /ɜː/ and party has /ɑː/.

4. A boy is a male child. To buy is to pay for something.

## Summary
• /ɜː/ is the vowel in birthday. /ɑː/ is the vowel in father and party.
• /ɔɪ/ is the vowel in boy and joy. /aɪ/ is the vowel in prize and invite.
• Hear the sound before you worry about the spelling.

studyPages.title: Lesson 2: The sounds /l/ and /r/ and celebration words
studyPages.body:
LESSON 2: THE SOUNDS /L/ AND /R/ AND CELEBRATION WORDS
======================================================

## What you will learn
• Hear and say /l/ and /r/ at the beginning of words.
• Use word wheels to build words such as load and road.
• Explain celebration words and use four of them in sentences.

Curriculum outcomes: a) discriminate sounds and words for listening, comprehension; b) pronounce words containing target sounds accurately for effective communication

## Introduction
If someone says "Turn light at the gate" when they mean "Turn right", the visitor walks the wrong way. The sounds /l/ and /r/ are different, and a celebration direction can depend on them.

## Notes

### How to make /l/
Put the tip of your tongue on the ridge behind your top teeth and let the air pass along the sides. Your voice is on. You hear /l/ at the start of load, light, play, balloon, colourful and celebrate.

### How to make /r/
Keep the tongue tip from touching that ridge. The tongue pulls back a little and the voice stays on. You hear /r/ at the start of road, right, pray, ribbon, present and prize.

Do not press your lips together for either sound. If /r/ starts to sound like /w/, smile slightly and keep the tongue busy.

studyPages.title: Lesson 2: The sounds /l/ and /r/ and celebration words — Word wheels
studyPages.body:
### Pairs that change meaning
- load and road
- light and right
- play and pray
- glass and grass
- lock and rock

Load means to put things onto a vehicle or a table. Road means the way vehicles travel. A wedding party can load gifts into a car and then travel on the road. Both words matter.

### Word wheels
A word wheel has a sound in the centre and letters around the edge. Join the centre to different letters to make words.

- Centre /l/: load, light, lock
- Centre /r/: road, right, rock
- Centre /ɔɪ/: boy, toy, joy
- Centre /aɪ/: my can be built by adding letters around the sound in prize, invite and night

studyPages.title: Lesson 2: The sounds /l/ and /r/ and celebration words — Words for family celebrations
studyPages.body:
### Words for family celebrations
- celebrate: to mark a special day with happy activities
- ceremony: a set of formal actions for an important event
- invitation: a request, spoken or written, asking someone to come
- wedding: the ceremony when two people marry
- birthday: the day each year that marks when a person was born
- burial: the ceremony of laying to rest a person who has died. Families gather, sing and comfort one another.
- feast: a large special meal
- graduation: a ceremony at the end of a level of school
- baptise: in many Christian families, a ceremony that welcomes a person, often a baby, with water
- decorate: to make a place look special
- Other useful words: ribbon, balloon, gift, present, card, cake, prize, song, joy

studyPages.title: Lesson 2: The sounds /l/ and /r/ and celebration words — Key words
studyPages.body:
A present and a gift can mean the same thing: something you give. A prize is something you win.

Use a word in a full sentence so its meaning shows: We will decorate the room with balloons and ribbons for the birthday party.

## Key words
• ceremony — a set of formal actions for an important event such as a wedding
• invitation — a request asking someone to come to an event
• feast — a large special meal for a celebration
• decorate — to add colours and objects that make a place look special

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Which word begins with /r/: balloon, ribbon, colourful, celebrate?

Working:
1. Balloon, colourful and celebrate begin with other sounds or have /l/.
2. Ribbon begins with /r/.

Answer: ribbon

## Worked examples

### Example 2
Use invitation and feast in one sentence about a wedding.

Working:
1. An invitation asks people to come.
2. A feast is the special meal.
3. Join them with a wedding.

Answer: Our invitation to the wedding said there would be a feast after the ceremony.

studyPages.title: Lesson 2: The sounds /l/ and /r/ and celebration words — Word wheels for /l/ and /r/
studyPages.body:
## Activity: Word wheels for /l/ and /r/
You will need: Paper circles divided into wedges, Pencils, A list of celebration words

1. In a group, draw two wheels. Write /l/ in the centre of one and /r/ in the centre of the other.

2. Around /l/ write load, light, lock, balloon and play. Around /r/ write road, right, rock, ribbon and prize.

3. Say each pair, load/road and light/right, and point to the wheel you hear when a partner says one word.

4. Choose four celebration words and each say a sentence that uses one of them.

studyPages.title: Lesson 2: The sounds /l/ and /r/ and celebration words — Answers to practice
studyPages.body:
## Practice

1. Write the /r/ partner of load, light and lock.

2. What is the difference between a gift and a prize?

3. Use the word decorate in a sentence about a birthday.

4. Which sound starts ribbon: /l/ or /r/?

## Answers to practice

1. road, right, rock

2. A gift is something you give to someone. A prize is something a person wins.

3. Any correct sentence, for example: We will decorate the room with balloons for the birthday party.

4. /r/

## Summary
• /l/ touches the tooth ridge. /r/ does not.
• Pairs such as load and road change meaning when the first sound changes.
• Celebration words include ceremony, invitation, feast, decorate, gift and prize.

studyPages.title: Lesson 3: Clear words in a celebration dialogue — A dialogue to listen to
studyPages.body:
LESSON 3: CLEAR WORDS IN A CELEBRATION DIALOGUE
===============================================

## What you will learn
• Pronounce target sounds in a short dialogue.
• Say why a wrong sound can confuse a listener.
• Role-play a celebration using the new words.

Curriculum outcomes: b) pronounce words containing target sounds accurately for effective communication; c) appreciate the importance of accurate pronunciation for effective communication

## Introduction
A family is planning a birthday. Every person in the plan must be heard correctly: who to invite, what to buy, and where to put the ribbons. Clear sounds keep the plan from falling apart.

## Notes

### A dialogue to listen to
Ask your teacher or a partner to read this aloud. Listen for /ɜː/, /ɑː/, /ɔɪ/, /aɪ/, /l/ and /r/.

Mother: We will have a party for your birthday.
Amina: May I invite my friends?
Mother: Yes. We can decorate the room with balloons and ribbons.
Father: I will buy a card and a gift. I will not forget the prize for the game.
Amina: Will there be a cake?
Mother: Yes, and we will sing a song. It will be a day of joy.
Father: Load the chairs onto the path, then carry them to the right side of the yard.

studyPages.title: Lesson 3: Clear words in a celebration dialogue — Why clear pronunciation matters
studyPages.body:
### Sounds in the dialogue
- party /ɑː/, birthday /ɜː/
- invite /aɪ/, buy /aɪ/, prize /aɪ/, right /aɪ/ and /r/
- joy /ɔɪ/
- balloons /l/, load /l/
- ribbons /r/, prize /r/, right /r/

Say the dialogue slowly, then at a natural speed. If you add the line "The boy will buy the balloons", keep boy and buy distinct.

### Why clear pronunciation matters
A listener cannot see your spelling. They only hear sounds. Load and road, light and right, boy and buy are different messages. At a celebration, the wrong word can send people, gifts or chairs to the wrong place.

Clear speech also shows respect. Guests who are older, younger, or visiting from another place should not have to struggle to understand you. Everyone's voice is a little different, and that is welcome. What we aim for is that the important sounds stay distinct.

studyPages.title: Lesson 3: Clear words in a celebration dialogue — Key words
studyPages.body:
### Subjects in these sentences
The key question for this theme also asks which words are used as subjects. In "Amina will invite her friends", Amina is the subject: she does the action. In "Father will buy a card", Father is the subject. The subject is usually the person or thing the sentence is about, and it often comes before the verb. Naming the subject clearly is part of speaking so that others understand.

### After you speak
When you role-play, face your partners, speak loudly enough for the group, and leave a pause at the full stop. If someone mishears right as light, repeat the word once, kindly, and show the direction with your hand.

## Key words
• dialogue — a conversation written so that each speaker has a turn
• subject — the person or thing that does the action in a sentence
• pronounce — to say a sound or word in a particular way

studyPages.title: Lesson 3: Clear words in a celebration dialogue — Example 2
studyPages.body:
## Worked examples

### Example 1
In the dialogue, who is the subject of "I will buy a card and a gift"?

Working:
1. The speaker of that line is Father.
2. I stands for Father.
3. Father is the person who will buy.

Answer: Father (the word I)

## Worked examples

### Example 2
A learner says "Turn light" but means the opposite of left. Which word should be used, and which sound starts it?

Working:
1. The opposite of left in a direction is right.
2. Right begins with /r/ and has the vowel /aɪ/.

Answer: right, beginning with /r/

studyPages.title: Lesson 3: Clear words in a celebration dialogue — Role-play the birthday plan
studyPages.body:
## Activity: Role-play the birthday plan
You will need: Copies of the dialogue, Simple props such as a card, a ribbon or a paper balloon, A phone or tablet only if the teacher is recording

1. Listen to the dialogue read aloud or played from an audio recording. List five words with the target sounds.

2. In groups of three, take the parts of Mother, Amina and Father and read the dialogue.

3. Add two new sentences that use celebration words, with a clear subject in each.

4. Role-play the scene. If the teacher agrees, record a short video and watch it to check the sounds /l/ and /r/ and the vowels /ɔɪ/ and /aɪ/.

5. Tell the class why saying load and road differently matters.

studyPages.title: Lesson 3: Clear words in a celebration dialogue — Answers to practice
studyPages.body:
## Practice

1. Name the target vowel in party and the target vowel in birthday.

2. From the dialogue, write one word with /l/ and one word with /r/.

3. Why should we pronounce sounds and words correctly at a celebration?

4. Who is the subject in "Amina will invite her friends"?

## Answers to practice

1. Party has /ɑː/. Birthday has /ɜː/.

2. Any correct pair, for example balloons (/l/) and ribbons (/r/).

3. So that listeners understand the right message. One wrong sound can change the word, as in light and right.

4. Amina

## Summary
• The dialogue practises /ɜː/, /ɑː/, /ɔɪ/, /aɪ/, /l/ and /r/ in real celebration words.
• A changed sound can change the meaning, so listeners need clear speech.
• The subject is the person or thing that the sentence is about.

studyPages.title: Revision quiz
studyPages.body:
REVISION QUIZ
=============

Answer all the questions, then mark yourself on the Answers tab.

1. Which word has the vowel /ɔɪ/?
   A. prize
   B. boy
   C. card
   D. birthday

2. Which pair contrasts /l/ and /r/?
   A. boy and toy
   B. load and road
   C. party and father
   D. night and prize

3. Which word begins with /r/?
   A. balloon
   B. celebrate
   C. ribbon
   D. colourful

4. The vowel in invite is ____.
   A. /ɜː/
   B. /ɑː/
   C. /ɔɪ/
   D. /aɪ/

5. What does feast mean?
   A. A written invitation
   B. A large special meal
   C. A prize won in a game
   D. A song sung at night

6. Choose the sentence that uses invitation correctly.
   A. We ate the invitation with a spoon.
   B. The invitation asked us to come to the wedding.
   C. He kicked the invitation into the goal.
   D. The invitation was a tall tree.

7. Why does saying light instead of right cause a problem?

8. Who is the subject in "Father will buy a card"?
   A. card
   B. buy
   C. Father
   D. a

9. Which word has /ɜː/?
   A. party
   B. start
   C. girl
   D. joy

10. Why is clear pronunciation a sign of respect at a family celebration?

studyPages.title: Quiz answers
studyPages.body:
ANSWERS
=======

1. B. boy
   Boy has /ɔɪ/. Prize has /aɪ/, card has /ɑː/, and birthday has /ɜː/.

2. B. load and road
   Load begins with /l/ and road begins with /r/.

3. C. ribbon
   Ribbon begins with /r/. The other words contain /l/.

4. D. /aɪ/
   Invite has the glide /aɪ/, the same vowel as prize and night.

5. B. A large special meal
   A feast is a large special meal, often part of a celebration.

6. B. The invitation asked us to come to the wedding.
   An invitation asks someone to attend an event.

7. The listener hears a different word and may go the wrong way or misunderstand the message.
   Light and right are different words because /l/ and /r/ are different sounds.

8. C. Father
   Father is the person who does the action.

9. C. girl
   Girl has /ɜː/, like birthday and turn.

10. Guests can understand you without struggling, including people who are younger, older or visiting.
   The aim is distinct sounds so the message is easy to follow.
